title: Anthropic asked the AI race to slow down.

slides.headline: Anthropic asked the AI race to **slow down.**
slides.sub: Dario Amodei’s three-part plan, what Anthropic committed to alone, and the one detail worth watching.

slides.headline: The pitch isn’t a pause. It’s a **speed limit.**
body: Amodei’s post argues capability gains must slow, especially AI that builds the next AI.
Two triggers: the OpenAI-HuggingFace breach, and models accelerating their own successors.
His line: progress will still seem fast. The point is to use the time you gain.
Three strategies. Anthropic is committing to one of them alone, starting now.

slides.quote: We must slow the pace at which we improve the **capabilities** of AI models. Progress will still seem fast.
slides.name: Dario Amodei

slides.headline: Three moves, ordered by **how real they are.**
items: Embed third-party evaluators inside the labs, now
Coordinate safety limits across democratic-country labs
Seek global bans on narrow uses, like bioweapons

slides.headline: Badges, desks, laptops. **Auditors inside.**
body: Evaluators from groups like METR get access on par with Anthropic’s internal risk teams.
The model is bank examiners: regulators who sit with the staff, not outside it.
Twenty years in the Air Force taught me the gap between a report and a resident inspector.
Amodei wants governments to require the same of every lab. Altman says OpenAI will follow.

slides.headline: The critics’ word for it: **regulatory capture.**
body: Brian Merchant’s read: it mostly serves Anthropic and OpenAI, the labs already out front.
Others say the doomsday framing distracts from harms the technology causes today.
Amodei’s answer: the benefits only arrive if the technology is built the right way.
Both can be true. Watch who gets a badge, and what they’re allowed to see.

slides.headline: Would you trust the report, or the **person inside?**
slides.sub: The plan lives or dies on evaluator access. Watch what “mostly comparable” turns out to mean in practice.
